Using Microsoft Graph API
with Windows PowerShell to

Monitor and Manage
Microsoft 365 Clients.

Microsoft Graph provides a unified
API layer across Microsoft Entra ID,

Intune, Microsoft 365, and security
services, making it the preferred

way to monitor users, devices,
compliance, and activity at scale.

In this video, we'll go over
how MSP technicians and IT

administrators can use Microsoft
Graph with Windows PowerShell

to monitor and manage
Microsoft 365 environments.

Before we begin, be sure to
subscribe to NinjaOne's IT video hub

and our YouTube channel for
more tech content like this.

How to Monitor and Manage M365
Clients with Microsoft Graph API.

In this next section, we'll provide
a high-level overview of common

Microsoft Graph API method so that
you get a sense of what's possible.

For full scripts, advanced
examples, and production-ready

automation workflows,
refer to our blog post.

Install Microsoft
Graph PowerShell SDK.

Make sure you're running
PowerShell 7 or later, have an

updated version of PowerShellGet,
have .NET Framework

4.7.2 or later installed,
and are using an execution
policy that allows signed scripts.

From there, open an elevated
PowerShell session and enter.

This installs the SDK without
impacting other user profiles,

which is ideal for shared
systems or jump boxes.

Connect to Microsoft
Graph PowerShell SDK.

Graph access is permission-based,
so connections should always

follow least-privilege
principles whenever possible.

To connect with read
access for users,

devices, and directories,
you can use.

You'll be prompted to authenticate
and consent to the requested scopes.
Graph also supports tenant-specific

connections and registered
app authentication.

Retrieve Device Information
and Compliance Status.

One of the most common Graph use
cases is Intune device visibility.

You can quickly retrieve managed
devices and their compliance state.

To examine device posture
across tenants, use this.

From there, filtering
for non-compliant devices

helps prioritize
remediation and reduce risk.
Monitor User Activity and Licensing.

User visibility is another area
where Graph excels: you can

retrieve users and assigned
licenses in a single query.

This command lists all users along
with their assigned licenses.

Graph also allows access
to sign-in records

when audit log
permissions are granted.

This is critical for
investigating suspicious activity.

Automate Remediation
and Policy Enforcement.

When combined with alerts
from RMM tools or Microsoft

Defender, Graph becomes a

You can also force MDM
enrollment or validate join

status using built-in
Windows commands.

These checks are
especially useful during

troubleshooting or
staged deployments.

Secure Token Usage with
GPO and Endpoint Controls.

On managed systems,
Local Group Policy can reduce

credential exposure by
preventing credential storage

and enforcing signed
PowerShell scripts.
This limits token theft, script

tampering,
and unauthorized automation.

Restricting script execution
to signed scripts ensures that

only trusted automation
runs on production systems.

When combined with PowerShell,
Microsoft Graph enables

scalable monitoring, automation,
and enforcement across

users, devices,
and security controls.

For more information, check
out our official blog post

on using Microsoft Graph API
with Windows PowerShell to

monitor and manage
Microsoft 365 clients,
linked in the description below.
